clue.text: Upset father by breaking flute

indicators.note: something broken has its parts scattered, so these letters come apart and are rearranged

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, as for a priest

explanation.surface: A dad gets upset when someone breaks his flute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as a verb, but it is the adjective definition. Fr is the title abbreviation for a priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fretful is anxious and agitated, which is what being upset means as an adjective.

clue.text: Formal borders, speaking of flowers

indicators.note: the borders of a word are its edges, so only its two outside letters are kept

blocks.note: oral means spoken, done by speaking

explanation.surface: A talk about formal flower beds and their borders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Formal borders' looks like garden beds, but it asks for the outside letters of 'Formal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Floral is the adjective describing anything made of or relating to blossoms and plants in bloom.

clue.text: Guy returning if accepted by centre left and groovy extremists

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards
what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside others
the centre of a word is its middle, so only the middle letters are kept
extremes are the ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A political tale of a man returning to a party of the centre left and some groovy radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a name, but a guy is the stuffed figure burnt on Bonfire Night in Britain, which is an effigy of Guy Fawkes.
explanation.definitionFit: A guy is the straw-filled dummy of Guy Fawkes burnt each November, a crude model of a person.

clue.text: Failed attempt to produce most counterfeit watercolours, for example

blocks.note: watercolour painting is an example of art

explanation.surface: A forger's bungled try at making fake watercolour paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: The split comes in an unexpected place: the superlative ends one letter after the first word of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A false start is a beginning that has to be abandoned, as when a runner jumps the gun, so an unsuccessful try.

clue.text: Large cars garaged by official I'm ostracising

indicators.note: a car that is garaged is kept inside a building, so the word sits inside these letters

explanation.surface: Someone shunning a bureaucrat who keeps big cars in a garage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garaged' suits the cars in the surface, but here it means kept inside the next few words.
explanation.definitionFit: Limos is the short form of limousines, long luxurious chauffeur-driven vehicles.

clue.text: 'Vacant' needed to follow punctuation mark in dictation

indicators.note: a vacant word has had its inside emptied out, leaving only the outer letters
following means coming after, so one piece is placed behind another

blocks.note: a comma is a punctuation mark

explanation.surface: A teacher dictating a passage tells pupils to put the word 'vacant' after a comma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacant' in quotes looks like a word to be written down, but it is the instruction to empty the word that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dictation in its sense of giving orders or authoritative instruction matches a command.

clue.text: Burn pieces of bacon, sire!

indicators.note: something in pieces is broken up, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: A cook apologising to a king for burning the bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces of bacon' sounds like rashers, but 'pieces of' is the signal to rearrange the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To carbonise something is to char it until only carbon remains, which is to scorch it thoroughly.

clue.text: Girl composed on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio things are heard rather than seen, so the answer sounds like the word

explanation.surface: A calm young woman being interviewed on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' looks like calm, describing the girl; it is the past tense of making something.
explanation.definitionFit: Maid is an old-fashioned or poetic word for a young unmarried woman.

clue.text: Jumble: coats, bra, tumblers

indicators.note: a jumble is a disordered heap, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A list of items at a jumble sale: coats, a bra and some drinking glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumble sale is a British charity sale of second-hand goods, and tumblers there would be glasses; here they are performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tumblers are gymnasts who perform somersaults and handsprings, the sort of performer seen in a circus.

clue.text: Sadly devastated about former lover I have difficulty in reading

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked, so the letters are thrown into a new order
about means around, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: Someone sadly heartbroken over an ex admits to struggling with reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' looks like an adverb on 'devastated', but it is the word to rearrange; the shuffled letters go round the ex and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyslexia is a learning condition that makes it hard to interpret written words and letters.

clue.text: Organs are not working with extra pedal ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: a machine that is off is not working
the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Church organs are broken, even with an additional pedal fitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sends you to church organs with pedals; the organs are the edible insides of an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the butchered internal parts of an animal, such as liver and kidneys, eaten as food.

clue.text: Outrageous drag is coming at the end of March carnival

indicators.note: something outrageous is wild and out of bounds, so the letters run wild into a new order
coming at the end places one piece after another

explanation.surface: Flamboyant drag queens appearing at the close of a carnival parade.
explanation.walkthrough: Drag performers suit the carnival scene, but 'drag is' supplies letters; the abbreviation for the month goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras is the Shrove Tuesday festival, celebrated with parades and costumes in New Orleans and Rio.

clue.text: Hostility among outsiders initially greeting mixed seniors

indicators.note: the outsiders of a word are its outermost letters, the first and last
initially means at the start, so only the first letter is kept
something mixed has been stirred together, so the letters change order

explanation.surface: Older people being unfriendly to newcomers who greet them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among' looks like a link between definition and wordplay, but its outside letters are part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggression is hostile, violent or confrontational behaviour toward others.

clue.text: Alumnus has extremely obscure pipe

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of a word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: A former student owns a pipe of a very obscure kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely obscure' reads as 'very obscure'; it takes the ends of the word. An old boy is the British term for a former pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboe is a woodwind instrument, and pipe is a general word for any wind instrument of that tubular kind.

clue.text: European capital's terror is linked to volcanic emissions

blocks.note: a little terror is a badly behaved child
lava is molten rock thrown out by a volcano

explanation.surface: A city's fear of an eruption from a nearby volcano.
explanation.walkthrough: The ''s' stands for 'is' and joins definition to wordplay; the following 'is' is part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bratislava is the capital city of Slovakia, on the Danube in central Europe.

clue.text: Tsk! Flipping tantrum routine and it's upturned ice cream

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read backwards
upturned means turned upside down, which in a down-the-page reading reverses the letters

blocks.note: tut and tsk are both sounds of disapproval
a rut is a dull fixed routine

explanation.surface: A tutting parent watches a child throw a tantrum and then knock over an ice cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse on the tantrum, but it is the instruction to turn the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti-frutti is an ice cream studded with chopped candied fruits of several kinds.

clue.text: Believers embracing alternative thinkers

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms round, so one piece surrounds another

explanation.surface: People of faith welcoming freethinkers with other views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alternative thinkers' looks like one phrase; 'alternative' is the conjunction, and 'thinkers' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Theorists are people who form abstract ideas and speculative explanations, so they are intellectuals at work.

clue.text: Can't turn in unusually rare hired vehicle

indicators.note: a turn twists things about, so these letters are rearranged
in places one piece inside another
unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters take an unexpected order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A driver unable to turn in an unusual hire car.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are rearranged, one placed inside the other; 'turn' looks like a driving manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: A rent-a-car is a car rented from a company for a short period, so a vehicle on hire.

clue.text: Eggy booze with turkey? That's a complete change of direction!

blocks.note: a flip is a drink of spirits or wine mixed with beaten egg
a turkey is a failure, as a show that flops

explanation.surface: Serving eggnog with the Christmas turkey would be a surprising U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey' suggests the festive bird but means a failure, as in a film that bombs.
explanation.definitionFit: A flip-flop is a sudden reversal of opinion or policy, especially by a politician.

clue.text: Stretching green mantle is out of order

indicators.note: things out of order are in the wrong sequence, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone protests that pulling a green cloak out of shape is not allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretching' reads as a verb, but it is a noun here, matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An enlargement is the act of making something bigger, as stretching makes a thing larger.

clue.text: Empty bistro and stuck-up old wine shop

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer letters
in a down clue something stuck up is placed upwards, so the letters read backwards

explanation.surface: A deserted restaurant beside a snooty, old-fashioned wine merchant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck-up' looks like snobbish, but in a down clue it means turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a Spanish wine cellar or shop selling wine, borrowed into English.

clue.text: Pay for rest

blocks.note: first meaning: to pay off a bill
second meaning: to come to rest or sit down

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like paying for some time off; the two words are separate meanings, joined by 'for'.
explanation.definitionFit: You settle a bill by paying it, and a bird settles on a branch when it comes down to rest.

clue.text: Error in copy taking turnover

indicators.note: in says the answer is sitting inside the following words
a turnover turns something over, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A mistake in a document about a company's turnover figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turnover' looks like business income, but it signals reading the run of letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A typo is a typing mistake, a small error made when keying in text.

clue.text: This sharpens good skin's colour

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
rind is the skin of fruit or cheese
a tone is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: An advert for a product that brightens a healthy complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharpens' reads as improving one's skin tone, but the definition is a tool that puts an edge on blades.
explanation.definitionFit: A grindstone is a revolving stone wheel used for honing knives and tools to a keen edge.

clue.text: Vikings coming from north or south-east

explanation.surface: Raiders sailing in from one direction or another.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points look like where the raiders came from, but they are just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse were the medieval Scandinavian seafaring peoples, so the name is a collective term for them.

clue.text: Part of remark needs a bit of articulation

indicators.note: part of a phrase means a piece sitting inside its letters

explanation.surface: A comment that needs to be spoken a little more clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulation' looks like clear speech, but it means a joint of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: An articulation is a joint where bones meet, and this one connects thigh to shin.

clue.text: Invasive presence in part of the bowel is extremely eager

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of a word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: the colon is the large intestine

explanation.surface: A medical note on a bacterium that is very keen to invade the gut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely eager' reads as 'very keen'; it takes the ends of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A coloniser takes over territory belonging to others, as an invading species or settler does.

clue.text: Quick signal

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an order to signal fast, but the two words are separate meanings, an adjective and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An alert person is quick to notice things, and an alert is a warning given to raise readiness.

clue.text: Hold down core pressure to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of these letters is used

explanation.surface: Advice on pressing down on the middle of something, a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core pressure' sounds like a physics term, but it simply houses the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To repress is to keep under control or subdue, as one keeps feelings or a rebellion in check.

clue.text: Discharge English bloke with a terrible fringe

indicators.note: a fringe is a border, so only the edge letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a bloke is British slang for a man

explanation.surface: An English man with a dreadful haircut is dismissed from his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fringe' looks like a hairstyle, but it means the edges of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or flow out from a source, as light or smell is sent forth.
